nameStory: The 'woodlouse' name comes from these little creatures' love of rotting wood, where they spend most of their lives munching on decaying matter. The 'shiny' part of their common name refers to their glossy, almost polished-looking shell that catches the light when they scurry across logs. Despite their name, they're not actually lice at all, but are more closely related to shrimp and crabs!
description: Common Shiny Woodlouses are small, gray armored creatures that look like tiny armadillos roaming around rotting logs and damp garden corners. These pill-bug relatives have segmented, oval bodies covered in a shiny, hard shell that's divided into distinct plates. They grow to about half an inch long and a quarter-inch wide, making them one of the larger woodlouse species you'll encounter. When disturbed, they use their seven pairs of legs to scurry quickly under cover.

idTips.label: Shiny shell texture
idTips.description: The body has a distinctly glossy, almost wet-looking surface that reflects light, feeling smooth and hard when gently touched

idTips.label: Segmented oval body
idTips.description: Body is clearly divided into overlapping armor-like plates, creating distinct ridges you can feel with your finger

idTips.label: Size and color
idTips.description: Relatively large for a woodlouse at about half an inch long, typically gray to dark gray with sometimes a brownish tint

idTips.label: Seven pairs of legs
idTips.description: Count the legs visible along the sides - you'll see seven pairs of small, jointed legs that move in a wave-like pattern

idTips.label: Cannot roll into ball
idTips.description: Unlike pill bugs, these flatten against surfaces when threatened but cannot curl into a complete ball

habitat: Look for Common Shiny Woodlouses under rotting logs, fallen branches, and leaf litter in deciduous and mixed forests throughout New England. They're especially common in damp areas near streams, in garden compost piles, and under loose bark of dead trees. You'll also find them in suburban settings - check under flower pots, garden stones, and even in basements or crawl spaces of houses.

seasonality.spring: Active as temperatures warm, emerging from winter hiding spots under deep leaf litter and logs. Look for them during warm, humid days when they're most active.
seasonality.summer: Most active during this season, especially after rain. Best viewing is in early morning or evening when they venture out to feed on decaying plant matter.
seasonality.fall: Still quite active as they prepare for winter, often found in large groups under the same log or stone. They're gathering in the dampest, most protected spots they can find.
seasonality.winter: Inactive and hidden deep under logs, stones, and leaf litter. In warmer spells, you might spot a few moving slowly in protected areas near buildings.

funFact: These little land-dwellers still breathe through gills just like their ocean-dwelling cousins, which is why they absolutely must stay moist - they're essentially marine animals that learned to live on land but never fully gave up their underwater breathing apparatus!
confusionNotes: Often confused with pill bugs (roly-polies), but pill bugs can roll into a perfect ball while woodlouses can only flatten out. Memory trick: 'Woodlouse won't roll, pill bug will ball.' Also distinguished from other woodlouse species by their notably shiny, reflective shell rather than the duller, matte finish of most relatives.
contextualKnowledge: Many people call all of these creatures 'pill bugs' or 'roly-polies,' but true pill bugs are actually a different family that can completely roll up. The name 'woodlouse' often makes people think they're related to lice, but they're actually crustaceans - more closely related to lobsters than to any insect.
compareHints: Since this is the only Oniscus species commonly found in New England, compare it to other woodlouse families by its distinctive glossy shell and larger size. Most other regional woodlouses have duller, more matte shells and are notably smaller. The shiny, almost metallic appearance is your best clue that you've found this particular species rather than the more common gray garden woodlouses.
